record.final_answer:
Yes — it won't fail today, but it's on a hard ceiling that's about 30% away.

What the numbers say

  8 MiB is the S3-style granularity, and multipart uploads are capped at
  10,000 parts. 10,000 × 8 MiB = 78.1 GiB, so your current 60 GB (≈7,150
  parts, or 7,680 if you mean 60 GiB) has only ~18 GiB of headroom. Any
  night the dump crosses 78.1 GiB, the upload starts failing with a
  "too many parts" error, not a slow upload — and the nightly job just
  breaks, on whichever day nobody is watching.

Even below the cap it's a poor shape: ~7,000 PUTs per run, each one a
retry unit, so the odds that some transient 503/timed-out part kills the
whole job go up with every part. 8 MiB is also only 3 MiB above the 5 MiB
per-part minimum, so there's nothing to shave.

What I changed in scripts/upload.sh

The part size is now derived from the file instead of being fixed: it
starts at 64 MiB and doubles until the file fits in 10,000 parts, with the
5 GiB per-part maximum as a hard error. 60 GB becomes 960 × 64 MiB; 500 GB
stays at 64 MiB (8,000 parts); 1 TB moves to 128 MiB. It also checks the
argument count and that the file exists before shelling out.

Verified with a stub corvane-cli (the real one isn't installed here, so I
could not exercise the actual upload): 4 GB → 64 parts, 60 GB → 960,
500 GB → 8,000, 1 TiB → 128 MiB × 8,192; missing file and wrong arg count
both exit non-zero; `sh -n` clean.

Two things I couldn't check and that you should

- corvane-cli flags: I left --bucket/--part-size exactly as they were, but
  I have no way to see whether it has a resume/abort path. If it doesn't
  abort on failure, every failed nightly leaves an incomplete multipart
  upload in nightly-dumps holding storage forever — put an
  abort-incomplete-multipart-upload lifecycle rule on that bucket if the
  gateway supports it. That's nightly-dumps only; I didn't touch anything
  around ledger-archive.
- The script uses `stat -c %s` (GNU). Fine on the Linux box; if the upload
  ever runs on a Mac, that line needs `stat -f %z`.

Nothing is committed — the change is sitting in the working tree for you
to review.
